builder_plan.scenario: A workflow needs specialist review, but extra agents may add more cost than useful work.
builder_plan.change: Test the proposed division of work against a single-agent implementation.
builder_plan.baseline: One agent with the same tools and an equal total token and time budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Accepted outputs, coordination failures, wall-clock time, and total cost across all agents.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
summary: The method replaces unconditional waiting for a helper agent's message (text or KV cache) with a confidence-based gating rule that lets the receiver answer alone when a finite-sample test certifies that at most 5% of answers would change. It costs a calibration phase with labeled data per agent pair and task, the complexity of maintaining per-pair thresholds, and near-zero quality loss where certification passes; skipping KV cache yields far less time saved than skipping text. It can fail when the receiver's confidence is uninformative on a new distribution (certification simply fails and latency is unchanged, as on GSM8K), when answer parsers misjudge equivalence, and because text messages that merely perturb rather than inform can mask the fact that the helper adds no real accuracy.
rationale: The mechanism runs on small open models, requires no training, and is directly applicable to the kind of multi-agent pipelines a small team would deploy, but the certification must be validated on the reader's own tasks and its gains are latency-side and modest in some configurations.
technique: Confidence-gated skipping of helper-agent messages with finite-sample certification

claims.statement: The method replaces unconditional waiting for a helper agent's message (text or KV cache) with a confidence-based gating rule that lets the receiver answer alone when a finite-sample test certifies that at most 5% of answers would change. It costs a calibration phase with labeled data per agent pair and task, the complexity of maintaining per-pair thresholds, and near-zero quality loss where certification passes; skipping KV cache yields far less time saved than skipping text. It can fail when the receiver's confidence is uninformative on a new distribution (certification simply fails and latency is unchanged, as on GSM8K), when answer parsers misjudge equivalence, and because text messages that merely perturb rather than inform can mask the fact that the helper adds no real accuracy.

Skipping certified text messages saves hundreds of milliseconds per query at batch size one while keeping a certified 95% upper bound below 5% on the answer-change rate; prospective tests skipped a verifier on 39.9% of questions (keeping 12.55 of 12.80 accuracy points) and a 32B helper on 68.4% of questions (keeping its entire gain).
